question: How many electrons can a molecule bind beyond its nuclear charge?
idea: In the stated nonrelativistic Coulomb model, the manuscript claims a molecule binds at most its total nuclear charge plus a universal constant times its number of nuclei. It also bounds neutral-atom ionization energies and specified outer radii, and gives asymptotic statements under particular large-charge limits.
why: Mathematics used to understand physical models, including quantum systems and interacting particles. A theorem concerns a specified model, not every physical situation.

glossary.meaning: A description of what happens as a size or parameter becomes very large.
A mathematical statement proposed to be true but requiring proof or a counterexample.

exactClaim: For the full nonrelativistic Coulomb model with two electron spin states, proves that a molecule with M fixed nuclei of charges at least one and total charge Z strictly binds at most $Z+CM$ electrons. Neutral-atom first ionization energies and radii containing all but an expected half-electron have universal positive upper and lower bounds. The energy cost of removing m electrons has Thomas–Fermi asymptotics as $m\to\infty$ and $Z/m\to\infty$; neutral-atom outer radii have the corresponding iterated-limit asymptotics, taking $Z\to\infty$ first. )
